title: Hezekiah's Faith Under Assyrian Threat
overview: Judah's king Hezekiah reforms worship and breaks free of Assyria, then faces that empire's army at Jerusalem's walls and a speech mocking his trust in the LORD.

parts.label: Hezekiah's reforms (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: Hezekiah shut down local hilltop shrines and objects tied to other gods, and even smashed the bronze snake from Moses' time because people were burning incense to it as if it were divine. The writer praises him as the most trusting of Judah's kings, and notes that he stopped paying tribute to Assyria and won back land from the Philistines.

parts.label: The northern kingdom falls (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, fell to Assyria after a three-year siege, and its people were carried off to distant lands. The writer explains this as the result of breaking their covenant, their binding agreement with God, and it sets up the danger now facing Judah from the same empire.

parts.label: Hezekiah pays to stop the invasion (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: When Assyria's king Sennacherib captured Judah's walled towns, Hezekiah admitted fault and paid an enormous sum, even stripping gold off the temple doors. Assyrian records and wall carvings of the siege of the Judean town of Lachish survive and broadly match this account.

parts.label: Assyria's envoy mocks Hezekiah (vv. 17-25)
parts.note: Three high Assyrian officials arrive with an army, and their spokesman ridicules Hezekiah's hope in Egypt as a cracked walking stick that stabs the hand leaning on it. He twists Hezekiah's reforms, suggesting that closing the local altars offended the LORD, and even claims the LORD sent Assyria to destroy Judah.

parts.label: Shouting to the people (vv. 26-35)
parts.note: Judah's officials ask him to speak Aramaic, the diplomatic language of the day, but he shouts in Hebrew so ordinary people on the wall will hear his crude warning of starvation and his offer of resettlement. His closing argument is that no nation's god has stopped Assyria, so the LORD will not either.

parts.label: Silence and torn clothes (vv. 36-37)
parts.note: The people obey the king's order not to answer. The officials tear their clothes, a common sign of grief and alarm, and report everything to Hezekiah, with the outcome left for the next chapter.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether Hezekiah's payment to Assyria was a lapse in the trust the chapter praises him for or a sensible move by a king protecting his people.
think: When someone powerful tells you that what you are relying on is foolish, how do you decide whether they have a point?
